To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the survival of Ixodes (I.) scapularis (Acari: Ixodidae) eggs was higher in woodlands of southeastern Canada than in a sand dune where ticks do not survive, 2) the survival of ticks in woodland habitats was associated with habitat characteristics and 3) the survival of eggs was predicted by remote-sensed data.

I. scacapularis populations can survive in woodland habitats in southeastern Canada, but survival varies among woodlands, and habitat classification and remote-sensed imagery may assist in identifying habitats in which ticks are likely to persist.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ecology and population biology of Ixodes ticks and the pathogens they transmit.
the ecology of Ixodes ticks and the transmission of Lyme disease in the Great Lakes region of Canada and the United States.
the ecology of I. scapiularis, and its potential for northward range expansion, in habitats of southeastern Canada.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the study provides evidence for the suitability of woodlot habitats in the Lower Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Plain for survival of I. scapiaris, and suggests that remote sensing data may be used to identify such habitats.
